narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: An experienced street dance educator with a focus on rhythm and body mechanics.
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Stationary Sprint
This is The Running Man. 1980s.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Title card: The Running Man · United States · 1980s

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Running Man emerged in the mid-1980s, with MC Hammer in Oakland, California, credited for its popularization.
A proto-version was documented in 1978 during a Fela Kuti concert in Berlin.
on_screen: Map: United States · North America
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a party dance, it evolved into a performance staple for concerts and music videos.
It serves as a display of rhythmic coordination and athletic style.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Run This Town SPOOF (https://archive.org/details/bliptv-20131012-221628-Alphacat-RunThisTownSPOOF892.)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dancer steps forward, then slides the front foot backward while moving fists horizontally in front of the body.
It mimics the motion of a stationary runner.
Watch for The Slide.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Stationary, performed in place.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Typically performed to 1980s and 1990s hip-hop and pop music.
The rhythm is usually a steady 4/4 beat that supports the repetitive nature of the sliding steps.
Listen for the Synthesizers, Drum machines, Electric bass.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 105 beats a minute.
Characterized by electronic percussion, heavy basslines, and a consistent, danceable pulse that emphasizes the downbeat.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Listen later: Rhythm Nation — Janet Jackson; Party Rock Anthem — LMFAO; Rhythm Nation 1814 — Janet Jackson (1989)
Waveform or rhythm-pattern graphic: Steady, driving beat with a strong downbeat.

scenes.title: The people
narration: MC Hammer, Janet Jackson, Paula Abdul, Bobby Brown, Five Star, Selena, Milli Vanilli, Vanilla Ice, Britney Spears, Scarlett Johansson, LMFAO.
The Roger Rabbit, popularized by Bobby Brown, is a variant that functions as a 'backwards' version of the Running Man.
The Running Man is a core hip-hop dance that influenced the Melbourne shuffle and various novelty fad dances.

scenes.title: Welcome
narration: Chapter 1 — First steps. Today: Master the slide.
Level: Beginner. Difficulty of the dance overall: beginner.
Your instructor: An experienced street dance educator with a focus on rhythm and body mechanics.
on_screen: Instructor front view, name of the chapter, the three things you will learn

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Slightly forward-leaning, athletic.
Fists move horizontally in front of the body.
Minimal movement, focus on leg and arm coordination.
on_screen: Instructor front then side view; freeze-frame on posture

scenes.title: Count and rhythm
narration: Count: 1-2-3-4-5-6. The meter is 4/4.
Rhythm pattern: Steady, driving beat with a strong downbeat..
Clap it first, then step it in place.
on_screen: Counts on screen, flashing on the beat
Metronome at 73 bpm
scenes.music: lesson_slow (clicks only until the step lands)

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
narration: Step 1: Stand with feet together.
Step 2: Lift one knee while sliding the standing foot backward.
Footwork from the sources: Shuffling and sliding steps.
Drill: Practice sliding one foot back while standing.
on_screen: Instructor front view, then back view (student's perspective); three repetitions
Counts on screen

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
narration: Step 3: Place the lifted foot down where the standing foot was.
Step 4: Repeat the motion with the opposite leg.
Drill: Add the knee lift.
on_screen: Instructor front and back view; slow, then half tempo

scenes.title: Put it together
narration: Step A, then Step B, without stopping. Slow first.
Now half tempo. Now full tempo.
Mirror: the instructor faces you and mirrors, so your right is your right.
Drill: Combine the slide and lift.
on_screen: Split screen: front view / back view
Tempo label changes: slow → half → full

scenes.title: Common mistakes and what to avoid
narration: Avoid losing balance by keeping the weight centered.
on_screen: Side-by-side: wrong / right

Options card: Seated or supported option: Perform the arm movements and knee lifts while seated in a sturdy chair. · For children: A 'follow the leader' game where children mimic the instructor's sliding steps.
